title: Mental factors
hookLine: fifty-two factors that color each moment of consciousness
last: RESULTS ARRIVE; KAMMA IS MADE IN THE RESPONSE.

cards: A white shirt goes into the wash with one red sock and comes out pink. Same water. Same shirt.
One small thing in the load, and everything has a new color. The Abhidhamma looks at a moment of mind in a similar way. In every moment there is a knowing, the plain fact of being aware of something.
And riding along with that knowing are things that tint it: interest, worry, kindness, hurry, ease.

teach.b: The Pali word is cetasika, a mental factor. A few days ago this path met citta, consciousness, the bare knowing that arises and passes moment by moment. A citta never comes alone.

The Abhidhammattha Sangaha, a manual of the Abhidhamma, describes a mental factor this way: it arises together with consciousness, ceases together with it, takes the same object, and rests on the same base.
Partners, not visitors who wander in on their own schedule. The same manual counts fifty-two of them, but the picture matters more than the number.
One moment of seeing a friend's face is seeing plus recognition, plus warmth, plus maybe a small reminder that a call is overdue. The seeing is the citta. What flavors it is cetasika.
The suttas have their own picture.

teach.h: A STAINED CLOTH TAKES DYE BADLY.
teach.b: In the Simile of the Cloth, the Buddha describes a cloth that is stained and dirty. Dip it in any dye, blue or yellow or red, and the color takes badly. Dip a clean cloth, and the color comes out clear.

In the same way, he says, when the mind is stained, an unhappy destination can be expected, and when it is clean, a happy one. The stains he names there include greed, ill will, anger, envy and conceit.
The Abhidhamma sorts lists like that carefully: which factors stain, which brighten, and which are present no matter what. Here's why that's useful.

teach.h: A MOOD IS A FACTOR IN A MOMENT.
teach.b: A mood, seen this way, is a factor in a moment, one dye among several. It arrived, and it can pass. Over the next days come the families: the factors in every moment, the troubled ones, and the beautiful ones.

how: Students of the Abhidhamma in Theravada communities learn the mental factors as named lists, often from the Abhidhammattha Sangaha, and some meditation teachers use the same names to help students note what is present in the mind.

o: the bare knowing itself, before any feeling arrives
the breath, which steadies every moment of mind
a mental factor that comes with knowing and colors it

games.q: what colors the mind: tap the pairs.
p: a factor that colors the knowing

s: a mental factor can arise on its own, without consciousness
the manual says a factor arises and ceases together with consciousness and takes the same object.
the Simile of the Cloth compares the mind to cloth taking dye
a stained cloth takes any dye badly; a clean one takes it clear.
in this way of seeing, a mood is simply who you are
a mood is one factor in a moment. it arrives, and it can pass.

games.q: you're a dyer with a pot of good blue dye and a cloth that is stained and dirty. what do you do?
o: dip it straight in; the dye will cover the stains.
clean the cloth first, then dye it.
use a darker dye to hide the stains.
games.why: in the Simile of the Cloth, a stained cloth takes any dye badly and a clean one takes it clear. the Buddha says the mind works the same way.

practice: If you'd like, look at this moment the way a dyer looks at cloth: there is knowing, a sound, the seat, the breath, and there is its color.

Name three colors quietly in plain words, like tired, curious, a little restless, without fixing any of them. Each one is a color on the knowing, not the knowing itself; if the colors change while you sit, name the new ones.

wordCard.voice: Cetasika. A mental factor: something that arises with each moment of consciousness and colors it. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali cetasika: a mental factor, arising and ceasing together with consciousness.

carryVoice: Your line: what colors the mind. The knowing goes on knowing; the colors keep changing. See you tomorrow.
